about: Hand-written annotations for the raw JSON-RPC exchange between the agent's host and the contract-repository server (stdio, newline-delimited JSON). Written by reading the captured frames, not generated. capture_wire.py refuses to write wire.json if any top-level field, or any field one level inside params/result, has no annotation here.
where_the_model_runs: The model call happens ONLY in the host process (agent_core/loop.py, the llm(prompt) call); it does NOT happen in the MCP client, on this wire (which carries tool names and arguments, never a prompt), or in the server, which cannot even ask for one because the client offers no `sampling` capability.
captured_with: scripts/wiretap.py between the agent's real McpHost and the server; raw = the exact line on the wire

frames.label: initialize.request
frames.what_it_is: Client -> server. The mandatory first message: 'here is who I am and what I can do; what about you?'

annotations.method: 'initialize' - the opening request of the handshake. No other request is legal until it has been answered and acknowledged.
annotations.params: The client's opening offer: the three fields below.
annotations.params.protocolVersion: The newest MCP spec revision this client speaks (2025-11-25). The server replies with the one version both sides will use.
annotations.params.capabilities: {} - the optional features this client offers the server (e.g. `sampling` = 'you may ask me to run an LLM', `roots`, `elicitation`). Empty, because our host offers none: server two has no way to make our host call a model.
annotations.params.clientInfo: Who is calling, for logs only. These are the SDK's defaults (name 'mcp', version '0.1.0') - not our agent's name and not a model name. The server learns nothing about which AI, if any, is behind the host.
annotations.jsonrpc: Protocol tag; always the literal string '2.0'. Every MCP message is a JSON-RPC 2.0 message.
annotations.id: 0 - the request id, chosen by the client (this SDK counts from 0). The server must echo it in its answer so the client can pair question and answer; a message with NO id is a notification and gets no answer.

frames.label: initialize.response
frames.what_it_is: Server -> client. The answer to initialize (same id): the server's identity and what it offers.

annotations.id: 0 - echoes the request's id; this is how the client knows this is the answer to #1.
annotations.result: Present instead of `error` because the request succeeded. Holds the three fields below.
annotations.result.protocolVersion: 2025-11-25 - the version the server agreed to speak. Had the server not supported the client's offer it would have answered with a version of its own and the client could disconnect.
annotations.result.capabilities: What this server offers. `tools` is present (listChanged:false = the tool list is fixed for the session, so the client need not re-list). `resources` and `prompts` are declared by the SDK by default; this server registers none. `experimental` is empty.
annotations.result.serverInfo: Server identity: name 'contract-repository'; version '1.30.0' is the version FastMCP reports (the SDK's), not a version of the knowledge team's code.

frames.label: initialized.notification
frames.what_it_is: Client -> server. One-way 'handshake complete, I am ready'. After this the session is open for normal requests.

annotations.method: 'notifications/initialized' - the client acknowledging the initialize result. A notification: it has no `id`, and the server sends no response.
annotations.jsonrpc: '2.0', as above. Note there is no `id` field at all - that absence is what makes this a notification rather than a request.

frames.label: tools_list.request
frames.what_it_is: Client -> server. Discovery: 'what tools do you have?' This is the message that makes adding a server a config-only change - the client asks instead of being told.

annotations.method: 'tools/list' - ask for the server's tool definitions.
annotations.id: 1 - next request id; the answer below must carry id 1.

frames.label: tools_list.response
frames.raw:
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"result":{"tools":[{"name":"get_contract","description":"Look up a contract by id and return its record: title, parties, status, execution date,
    confidentiality class, original effective date, and how many amendments are on file.","inputSchema":{"properties":{"contract_id":{"title":"Contract Id","type":"string"}},"required":["contract_id"],"title":"get_contractArguments","type":"object"},"outputSchema":{"properties":{"result":{"title":"Result","type":"string"}},"required":["result"],"title":"get_contractOutput","type":"object"}},{"name":"get_effective_date","description":"Return the effective date of a contract. With no `as_of`, returns the original effective
    date and the latest version's. With `as_of` (YYYY-MM-DD), returns the version in force on
    that date.","inputSchema":{"properties":{"contract_id":{"title":"Contract Id","type":"string"},"as_of":{"anyOf":[{"type":"string"},{"type":"null"}],"default":null,"title":"As Of"}},"required":["contract_id"],"title":"get_effective_dateArguments","type":"object"},"outputSchema":{"properties":{"result":{"title":"Result","type":"string"}},"required":["result"],"title":"get_effective_dateOutput","type":"object"}},{"name":"get_amendment_chain","description":"Return a contract's amendment chain in order: the original, then each amendment with its
    effective date, the clause range after it, and a one-line summary of what it changed.","inputSchema":{"properties":{"contract_id":{"title":"Contract Id","type":"string"}},"required":["contract_id"],"title":"get_amendment_chainArguments","type":"object"},"outputSchema":{"properties":{"result":{"title":"Result","type":"string"}},"required":["result"],"title":"get_amendment_chainOutput","type":"object"}}]}}

tools.name: get_contract
tools.description:
Look up a contract by id and return its record: title, parties, status, execution date,
    confidentiality class, original effective date, and how many amendments are on file.

tools.name: get_effective_date
tools.description:
Return the effective date of a contract. With no `as_of`, returns the original effective
    date and the latest version's. With `as_of` (YYYY-MM-DD), returns the version in force on
    that date.

tools.name: get_amendment_chain
tools.description:
Return a contract's amendment chain in order: the original, then each amendment with its
    effective date, the clause range after it, and a one-line summary of what it changed.

frames.what_it_is: Server -> client. The tool catalogue. The host turns each entry into a line of the model's prompt, so this one message is the entire 'wiring' of server two into the agent.

annotations.result: Success payload. Its only field here is `tools`; a `nextCursor` field, if present, would mean more pages follow - its absence means this is the last page.
annotations.result.tools: Array of tool definitions: get_contract, get_effective_date, get_amendment_chain - three tools, which is the 'after' count minus server one's three.
annotations.result.tools[].name: The identifier used in tools/call. Names are how the host routes a model's choice back to this server.
annotations.result.tools[].description: The docstring, verbatim including its source indentation. This text is placed into the model's prompt, so for the model it IS the tool's documentation - which is why requirement 5 treats a docstring as a prompt.
annotations.result.tools[].inputSchema: JSON Schema for the arguments, generated by the SDK from the Python type hints (contract_id: required string; as_of: optional string). The server validates calls against it; the host also prints it to the model as the argument list.
annotations.result.tools[].outputSchema: SDK-generated schema saying the structured result is an object {result: string}, because the function returns a str. Our host does not use it.

frames.label: tools_call.request
frames.what_it_is: Client -> server. The only message in this exchange whose content came from a model's decision: the host parsed the model's JSON action into tool name + arguments and sent this. No prompt travels with it.

annotations.params: The call: the two fields below.
annotations.params.name: 'get_amendment_chain' - must be a name the server advertised in tools/list. The host looked up which server owns this name and sent the call to that one.
annotations.params.arguments: {contract_id: 'MSA-2021-0142'} - the values the model chose, checked by the server against inputSchema. The server sees values only: not the question, not the prompt, not which model.
annotations.id: 2 - next request id; the answer must carry id 2.

frames.label: tools_call.response
frames.what_it_is: Server -> client. The tool's output. The host wraps `content` as untrusted data and appends it to the model's history for the next model call.

annotations.result: Success at the protocol level (a tool that fails still returns `result`, with isError true; a JSON-RPC `error` member is reserved for protocol faults such as an unknown method).
annotations.result.content: Array of content blocks - what the model reads. Here one text block holding the amendment chain as JSON text. Plain data: no model produced it.
annotations.result.content[].type: 'text' - the block kind (others: image, audio, resource). Our host keeps text and notes any other kind as omitted.
annotations.result.content[].text: The payload itself: the amendment chain Original (2021-04-01) -> Amendment 1 (2022-01-01) -> Amendment 2 (2023-06-01).
annotations.result.structuredContent: The same payload as a machine-readable object, wrapped as {result: ...} to match outputSchema. Duplicate of `content` for this tool; our host ignores it and uses `content`.
annotations.result.isError: false - the tool ran. When true, `content` carries the failure text and that text is the ONLY thing the model gets to recover from - which is why error wording matters (requirement 5).
